status: drafted via multi-agent workflow, adversarially fact-checked and corrected
notes: Titus is a short, thin-narrative pastoral epistle (3 chapters, 46 verses) — almost entirely direct instruction from Paul to his delegate Titus, left to organize the young churches of Crete, rather than a book with scenes and action beats. Only two figures are personally embodied across the letter: Paul (the writer, making real decisions — where to send Artemas/Tychicus, where to winter, whom to provision) and Titus (the addressee, personally charged to ordain elders, teach, and later travel to Nicopolis). Everything else in the letter's body is teaching content, so six law/theme tiers carry the bulk of the book: elder qualifications (1:5-9), the warning about corrupt Cretan teachers (1:10-16), household-wide sound doctrine for aged men/women, young men/women, and servants (2:1-10), the grace-of-God doctrine that grounds that ethic (2:11-15), the civic-obedience-and-regeneration doctrine of 3:1-8 (extended through the closing general instruction of 3:14, which continues its "maintain good works" theme by way of the Zenas/Apollos provisioning example), and the closing instruction on avoiding contentious questions and disciplining a heretic (3:9-11). All six are deliveredBy Paul, since he is the one writing/relaying every line of this letter to Titus. Four named companions appear only in the closing personal notes (3:12-13) with a single verse of action each — Artemas, Tychicus, Zenas the lawyer, and Apollos — none of whom carries enough independent narrative weight to be a manager in this book, so all four are submanagers under Paul with a loyalty-boost flavor (fellow workers in his mission, not opposition). Every verse in the book (1:1 through 3:15) is now accounted for across the eight tiers and Paul's own verse list. Naming-collision/attribution notes: the unnamed "prophet of their own" quoted in 1:12 ("The Cretians are alway liars...") is traditionally identified with the Cretan poet Epimenides by later scholarship, but Titus itself never names him — flagged as tradition, not textual fact, per the project's naming-collision/traditional-name discipline. Tychicus and Apollos are well-attested elsewhere in the NT (Ephesians, Colossians, 2 Timothy for Tychicus; Acts 18 and 1 Corinthians for Apollos) but their ids here are suffixed "_titus" since only this book's single-verse mention is indexed in this pass — fuller entries for those books are out of scope here. No character in this book has any scripturally-stated age, so every ageEvents array is empty, and genealogy fields are left null throughout since Titus itself states no family relationships for anyone in it. Law-tier "purpose" fields were revised during fact-check to describe what each passage actually says rather than adding interpretive theological framing (e.g. grace-vs-legalism, gratitude-vs-self-righteousness) not literally present in the text.

scribeTiers.scribeName: The Elders Ordained in Every City

characters.name: Paul

verses.note: Opens the letter identifying himself as 'a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect, and the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness.'
Describes the hope of eternal life 'promised before the world began' and now manifested through the preaching 'committed unto me according to the commandment of God our Saviour.'
Greets Titus as 'mine own son after the common faith: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour.'
States his purpose in leaving Titus in Crete: 'to set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city.'
Plans to send Artemas or Tychicus to Titus, and instructs Titus to then come to him at Nicopolis, 'for I have determined there to winter.'
Instructs Titus to 'bring Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that nothing be wanting unto them.'
'And let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful' — extends the instruction to provision Zenas and Apollos into a general principle for believers.
Closes the letter: 'They that are with me salute thee. Greet them that love us in the faith. Grace be with you all. Amen.'

funFacts: Titus does not state Paul's family background (compare Philippians 3:5, Acts 22:3, not part of this book) — omitted here rather than imported from elsewhere.
The letter's greeting (1:1-4) is unusually doctrinal for its length compared with Paul's other openings, packing a full statement on the hope of eternal life into the salutation itself.

characters.name: Titus

verses.note: Addressed by Paul as 'mine own son after the common faith,' receiving the letter's grace/mercy/peace greeting.
Left by Paul in Crete 'that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city.'
Instructed: 'But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine.'
Told to show himself 'a pattern of good works: in doctrine shewing uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity, sound speech, that cannot be condemned.'
Instructed to 'speak, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no man despise thee.'
To be diligent to come to Paul at Nicopolis once relieved by Artemas or Tychicus, and to help Zenas and Apollos on their way first.

funFacts: Titus's own Gentile/Greek identity is stated in a different epistle (Galatians 2:3 — 'neither Titus...being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised'), not in this book itself, so it is noted here only as a cross-reference, not indexed as content of Titus.

characters.name: The Elders Ordained in Every City
characters.scribeTier: The Elders Ordained in Every City
characters.purpose: Establishes the moral and spiritual qualifications an elder/bishop must meet, so the newly-planted Cretan churches have trustworthy leaders able to teach sound doctrine and refute error rather than repeat it.

verses.note: States the reason elders are needed in every city.
An elder must be blameless, husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly.

A bishop, as steward of God, must be blameless — not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre — but a lover of hospitality, good men, sober, just, holy, temperate.
Must hold fast the faithful word as taught, able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince gainsayers.

characters.name: The Unruly and Vain Talkers
characters.purpose: Warns Titus about corrupt teachers subverting whole households in Crete for dishonest gain, and instructs him to rebuke them sharply so the churches stay sound in the faith.

verses.note: Notes 'many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision.'
Says their mouths must be stopped, since they subvert whole houses, teaching things they ought not for filthy lucre's sake.
Quotes 'one of themselves, even a prophet of their own,' saying 'The Cretians are alway liars, evil beasts, slow bellies.'
Calls the witness true and instructs Titus to 'rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith; not giving heed to Jewish fables, and commandments of men, that turn from the truth.'
'Unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled...is nothing pure'; such 'profess that they know God; but in works they deny him.'

funFacts: The unnamed 'prophet of their own' quoted in 1:12 is traditionally identified by later commentators with the Cretan poet Epimenides — but the text of Titus itself never names him, so that identification is flagged here as tradition, not textual fact.

characters.name: Sound Doctrine for the Household
characters.purpose: Orders godly conduct across every age and station within the church — aged men and women, young men and women, and servants — so that the doctrine of God is adorned rather than blasphemed before outsiders.

verses.note: Opens the section: 'speak thou the things which become sound doctrine.'
Aged men to be sober, grave, temperate, sound in faith, in charity, in patience.
Aged women to be 'in behaviour as becometh holiness,' not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things.
The aged women are to teach young women to love their husbands and children, to be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, 'that the word of God be not blasphemed.'
Young men exhorted to be sober-minded.

Servants (bondservants) instructed to be obedient to their own masters, not answering again, not purloining, but showing good fidelity, that they may 'adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.'

characters.name: The Grace That Bringeth Salvation
characters.purpose: Describes the grace of God that has appeared to all men, teaching the denial of ungodliness and worldly lusts and a sober, righteous, godly life, while looking for the blessed hope of Christ's appearing and recalling that he gave himself to redeem and purify a people for himself — following directly after the household instructions of chapter 2.

verses.note: 'For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men.'
That grace teaches denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, and living soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world.
Describes 'looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ.'
Christ 'gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.'
Closes with the instruction to speak, exhort, and rebuke with all authority.

characters.name: Washing of Regeneration
characters.purpose: States instructions to be subject to rulers, obey magistrates, and be gentle toward all men; recalls what believers were before — foolish, disobedient, deceived — then describes salvation as coming not by works of righteousness but according to God's mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Ghost poured out through Jesus Christ, so that being justified by his grace they are made heirs according to the hope of eternal life; closes by affirming that believers should be careful to maintain good works, extended in 3:14 into a general instruction that 'ours' likewise learn to maintain good works for necessary uses.

verses.note: Reminds them to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, and to be ready to every good work.
To speak evil of no man, be no brawlers, but gentle, showing all meekness unto all men.
'For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.'

'The kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared, not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost.'
The Holy Ghost shed on believers abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour, 'that being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.'
'This is a faithful saying...that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works.'

characters.name: Foolish Questions and the Heretic
characters.purpose: Preserves unity in the young Cretan churches by warning against divisive, speculative controversies and prescribing a clear discipline process for a persistently false teacher.

verses.note: 'Avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.'
'A man that is an heretic after the first and second admonition reject.'
Explains such a man 'is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself.'

characters.name: Artemas
characters.perkNote: Named only this once in the entire New Testament — no other appearance to cross-reference.

verses.note: One of two men (with Tychicus) Paul considers sending to Crete to relieve Titus so Titus can travel to Nicopolis.

characters.name: Tychicus
characters.perkNote: The same Tychicus appears more fully elsewhere as a trusted courier (Ephesians 6:21, Colossians 4:7, 2 Timothy 4:12) — only his single mention within Titus itself is indexed here, id suffixed to keep this book-scoped entry distinct.

verses.note: The other of the two men Paul considers sending to relieve Titus in Crete.

characters.name: Zenas the Lawyer
characters.perkNote: Named only this once in the entire New Testament; the text calls him 'the lawyer' without further specifying whether this means a Jewish legal scholar or a Roman-trained jurist.

verses.note: Paul instructs Titus to 'bring Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that nothing be wanting unto them.'

characters.name: Apollos
characters.perkNote: The same Apollos appears more fully elsewhere (Acts 18:24-28, 1 Corinthians 1/3/4/16) as an eloquent teacher mighty in the scriptures — only his single mention within Titus itself is indexed here, id suffixed to keep this book-scoped entry distinct.

verses.note: Sent along with Zenas the lawyer; Titus is told to see that nothing is lacking for their journey.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk or deliberately-unresolved references kept out of the character list above.

cretians_collective.note: The corrupt teachers and the broader Cretan populace quoted in 1:12 are addressed collectively (see the 'cretian_liars' law-tier character) — the text does not individuate them into named persons, so none are broken out as separate character entries.

titus_cross_book_background.note: Titus's Gentile/Greek identity and his presence with Paul at the Jerusalem council are stated in Galatians, not in Titus itself — logged here as a pointer only, not imported as content of this book.
